milestones.title: counting parameters
milestones.task: Write head_dim, attn_params, mlp_params (one expert), norm_params, block_params(cfg, active=False), embedding_params and count_params(cfg, active=False). The Config fields are documented in the starter: mlp is "swiglu" or "gelu", norm is "rms" or "layer", and bias, tied, positions, experts and top_k default to the Llama-style values.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the parts of Llama 3 8B and GPT-2 small by hand (41,943,040 attention weights, 176,160,768 MLP weights, 4,722,432 for a biased GELU MLP), the exact totals of six models, the active count of Mixtral, then 60 seeded random model shapes against a counter that lists every weight tensor of the model and adds up their sizes, and finally the table of eight published sizes.
milestones.explain:
A parameter is one learned number, and nearly all of them live in matrices, so counting them is multiplying shapes. Chapter 16 gave the recipe for a modern decoder, and this milestone writes it as six small functions so that each term can be tested alone:

  • Attention has four matrices: Wq and Wo are C × C, and Wk, Wv are C × (KV · dk). With grouped-query attention (GQA, chapter 19) there are fewer key/value heads than query heads (8 against 32 for Llama 3 8B), so the keys and values are a quarter as wide and the attention block shrinks from 4C2 to 2.5C2. Older models like GPT-2 and Llama 2 7B have KV = H.
  • The MLP has three C × F matrices for a SwiGLU (gate, up, down; chapter 10) and two for a GELU MLP. GPT-style models use F = 4C; Llama-style models pick F so that the three matrices cost about the same as two with 4C.
  • Norms add C weights per RMSNorm (Llama) or 2C per LayerNorm with a bias (GPT-2), two per block and one at the end. Biases, if the model has them, add a vector per projection.
  • Embeddings are a V × C table for the input; the output head is another V × C unless it is tied to the input table (GPT-2 ties, Llama 3 does not). GPT-2 also has a learned table of position vectors.
  • A mixture of experts (chapter 20) replaces the one MLP by E of them and a small router (C × E weights) that picks top_k for each token. The model stores E MLPs but each token uses only top_k of them, so there are two honest answers to "how many parameters", and the function takes active=True for the second.

Here is what the finished functions say about Llama 3 8B, the model whose 8,030,261,248 weights chapter 16 counted by hand:

import solution as m
c = m.MODELS["Llama 3 8B"]
n = m.count_params(c)
parts = {"attention": c.L * m.attn_params(c), "MLP": c.L * m.mlp_params(c), "norms": c.L * m.norm_params(c) + c.C,
         "embeddings": m.embedding_params(c)}
print(f"Llama 3 8B: {n:,} parameters")
for k, v in parts.items():
    print(f"  {k:<11}{v:>15,}  {v / n:6.1%}")
print(f"  parts add up: {sum(parts.values()) == n}")
g = m.MODELS["GPT-2 small"]
print(f"GPT-2 small: {m.count_params(g):,}  (embeddings are {m.embedding_params(g) / m.count_params(g):.0%} of it)")
x = m.MODELS["Mixtral 8x7B"]
print(f"Mixtral 8x7B: {m.count_params(x):,} stored, {m.count_params(x, active=True):,} used per token")
Llama 3 8B: 8,030,261,248 parameters
  attention    1,342,177,280   16.7%
  MLP          5,637,144,576   70.2%
  norms              266,240    0.0%
  embeddings   1,050,673,152   13.1%
  parts add up: True
GPT-2 small: 124,439,808  (embeddings are 32% of it)
Mixtral 8x7B: 46,702,792,704 stored, 12,879,925,248 used per token

Notice three things. The MLP is 70% of the weights and attention only 17%, the pattern chapter 16 pointed out. Norms are a rounding error (266,240 weights), which is why people ignore them in back-of-envelope counts. And embeddings are a third of GPT-2 small but only 13% of Llama 3 8B, which is why a "non-embedding parameter count" (Kaplan et al., 2020) differs from the full count by a third for small models and hardly at all for large ones.

The published models

The last test in the checker is a table of eight models against the sizes in their papers and model cards. It is where you find out whether your formula describes reality:

ModelCountedPublishedSource of the shape
GPT-2 small124,439,808124 MReleased config: 768 wide, 12 layers, 12 heads, 1,024 positions; tied head, biases, LayerNorm
GPT-3 175B174,604,259,328175.0 BBrown et al. (2020), Table 2.1: 96 layers, 12,288 wide, 96 heads, dff = 4 dmodel, 2,048 context
Llama 2 7B6,738,415,6166.7 BReleased config: 32 layers, 4,096 wide, F = 11,008, V = 32,000
Llama 3 8B / 70B / 405B8.03 B / 70.55 B / 405.85 B8 B / 70 B / 405 BLlama 3 paper, Table 3; V = 128,256 in the release
Mixtral 8x7B46,702,792,704 (12,879,925,248 active)46.7 B (12.9 B)Released config: 8 experts, 2 per token, 8 key/value heads
Chinchilla 70B64,951,435,26470 BHoffmann et al. (2022), Table 4: 80 layers, 64 heads, 8,192 wide, dff = 4 dmodel

Seven of the eight agree with the published figure to within 1% (the differences are rounding in the model names: "8B" for 8.03 billion, "70B" for 70.55). The odd one is Chinchilla: counting its published table gives 64.95 billion, 7.2% below the "70B" in its name. The checker allows 10% for it and prints the gap. The gap is 5.05 billion weights, close to 80 × 8,1922 = 5.37 billion, which is the size of one extra C × C matrix in each of the 80 layers. Chinchilla uses Gopher's architecture, and my hypothesis is that the extra matrices are Gopher's relative-position weights, but I have not verified that against the papers, so treat it as a lead and not a fact. The practical lesson stands either way: a count from a configuration is an estimate to be checked, and "70B" is a name, not a measurement.

Common misconception

"A model's parameter count is the number in its name." Names are rounded and sometimes loose, and papers disagree about what to count: with or without embeddings, with or without every expert, with or without the output head if tied. A scaling-law constant fitted with non-embedding N does not transfer to a formula that uses the total. Whenever you reuse a number, ask which N it is.

milestones.title: FLOPs, time and cost
milestones.task: Write matmul_flops, matmul_weights, train_flops_per_token(cfg, T), rule_6nd, train_flops(cfg, tokens, T), train_seconds(flops, peak, mfu, n_gpus=1), gpu_hours and mfu_from_throughput.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks matmul_weights for Llama 3 8B (7,504,658,432), the ratios 1.001, 1.202 and 5.213 of chapter 16 and 1.078 for the 405B at 8,192 tokens, that the score term grows by exactly 12LC per extra context token, the 3.8 × 1025 FLOP budget, 67.8 days and 26.7 million GPU-hours for the 405B plan, 16.6 GPU-hours for GPT-2 small on 10 billion tokens, that GPU-hours do not depend on the number of GPUs, and, on 40 seeded random dense shapes, that matmul_weights equals the active parameters minus norms and the input table.
milestones.explain:
A FLOP is one floating-point operation, an addition or a multiplication, and the work of a run is counted in them. The whole count rests on one formula: multiplying an (m, k) matrix by a (k, n) matrix makes m × n outputs, each a sum of k products, so 2mkn FLOPs. Applied to a linear layer on n tokens that is 2 FLOPs per weight per token on the forward pass, and the backward pass needs two such products (one for the weight gradient, one for the input gradient), so 4 more. A training run over D tokens therefore costs about 6ND FLOPs, where N counts the weights that take part in matrix products (chapter 16 derives this and checks it by instrumenting a real forward and backward pass).

Two refinements make the calculator more honest than the rule of thumb, and both are in chapter 16:

  • Which weights count. The input embedding is a lookup, not a product, so it costs no FLOPs; the output head is a product and does. Norms and biases are a few operations per number, not matrix products. For a mixture of experts only the top_k active experts' matrices are multiplied. matmul_weights captures this, and for a dense model it is the active parameter count minus norms and the input table (the checker verifies exactly that on random shapes).
  • The attention scores have no weights. Q·KT and (softmax weights)·V are matrix products between activations. For a context of T tokens they add 12 · L · C · T FLOPs per training token (4TC per layer forward, three times that with the backward pass), a term that grows with context while the weight term does not. It is small at T = 2,048 and dominant at 128K.
import solution as m
c = m.MODELS["Llama 3 8B"]
N = m.count_params(c)
print("Llama 3 8B: training FLOPs per token, exact count against 6N")
for T in (2048, 8192, 131072):
    f = m.train_flops_per_token(c, T)
    score = 12 * c.L * c.C * T
    print(f"  T={T:>6}  exact {f:.3e}  6N {6 * N:.3e}  ratio {f / (6 * N):5.3f}  attention-score share {score / f:5.1%}")
big = m.MODELS["Llama 3 405B"]
flops = m.rule_6nd(m.count_params(big), 15.6e12)
H100 = m.GPUS["H100 SXM"]["peak"]
print(f"405B on 15.6T tokens: 6ND = {flops:.2e} FLOPs")
for mfu in (0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5):
    print(f"  MFU {mfu:.0%}: {m.train_seconds(flops, H100, mfu, 16384) / 86400:6.1f} days on 16,384 H100s, {m.gpu_hours(flops, H100, mfu) / 1e6:5.1f}M GPU-hours")
Llama 3 8B: training FLOPs per token, exact count against 6N
  T=  2048  exact 4.825e+10  6N 4.818e+10  ratio 1.001  attention-score share  6.7%
  T=  8192  exact 5.791e+10  6N 4.818e+10  ratio 1.202  attention-score share 22.2%
  T=131072  exact 2.512e+11  6N 4.818e+10  ratio 5.213  attention-score share 82.1%
405B on 15.6T tokens: 6ND = 3.80e+25 FLOPs
  MFU 20%:  135.7 days on 16,384 H100s,  53.3M GPU-hours
  MFU 30%:   90.4 days on 16,384 H100s,  35.6M GPU-hours
  MFU 40%:   67.8 days on 16,384 H100s,  26.7M GPU-hours
  MFU 50%:   54.3 days on 16,384 H100s,  21.3M GPU-hours

The first block reproduces chapter 16's table: at 2,048 tokens 6N is accurate to 0.1%, at 8,192 it is 20% low for the 8B shape, and at 131,072 tokens attention scores are 82% of the arithmetic. The second block is the credibility check of the whole method: 6 × 405.85 billion × 15.6 trillion is 3.80 × 1025 FLOPs, the figure Meta reports for pre-training Llama 3 405B.

FLOPs are the same on any hardware; time is FLOPs divided by the speed you actually get. A GPU's datasheet gives a peak (989 TFLOP/s dense bf16 for an H100 SXM, 312 for an A100), and a real run reaches a fraction of it, the model FLOPs utilisation (MFU) of PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022): the model FLOP/s you actually deliver, divided by peak. Well-tuned large runs land at 30% to 50%. So

seconds = FLOPs / (peak × MFU × number of GPUs),   GPU-hours = FLOPs / (peak × MFU) / 3600

The MFU rows of the output are the single most useful result in the milestone: the same 405B plan takes 135.7 days at 20% and 54.3 days at 50%. A guess of "about 40%" is the biggest source of error in a schedule, so you want it to be a measurement. This is a calculation, not a report of how long Meta's run took; real runs also lose time to failures and restarts (A3 chapter 05).

State of play, October 2026

The two peak figures in GPUS (312 TFLOP/s for the A100, 989 TFLOP/s for the H100 SXM, dense bf16) are from vendor datasheets and describe two widely deployed generations; newer accelerators have more memory, higher bandwidth and lower-precision formats with much higher quoted peaks, and their prices and the MFU that real code reaches on them change with each software release. Take current figures from the datasheet of the exact part, and MFU from a measurement of your own code. Prices are deliberately not in the starter file: cost is GPU-hours times whatever you pay, and that number is yours to supply.

milestones.title: memory for training
milestones.task: Write state_bytes(n, weights=2, grads=2, master=4, m=4, v=4), act_bytes_per_layer(s, b, h, a, mode) (modes "full", "flash", "recompute"; anything else raises ValueError), activation_bytes(cfg, s, b, mode), training_memory(cfg, s, b, mode) (a dict with keys states, activations, total), fits(total_bytes, gpu_mem, overhead=3e9), max_microbatch(cfg, s, mode, gpu_mem) and max_trainable_params(gpu_mem).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks 16 bytes per parameter and the 8-bit variant, the three activation formulas on hand values (312, 272 and 16 bytes for s = 2, b = 1, h = 4, a = 2), the 12 entries of chapter 16's table to within 1%, that activations scale linearly with the microbatch and the score term quadratically with the sequence, the boundary of fits, and max_microbatch for a 1B-class model on a 24 GB card in all three modes against a brute-force search.
milestones.explain:
Compute decides how long a run takes; memory decides whether it starts. GPU memory is a hard wall: when the total exceeds the card, the job stops with an out-of-memory error. Training holds two kinds of memory, and they are best counted separately.

Model states depend only on the parameter count. Mixed-precision training with AdamW (A0 chapter 10; chapter 17) keeps five numbers per parameter: a bf16 weight (2 bytes), a bf16 gradient (2), an fp32 master copy of the weight (4) and Adam's two running averages in fp32 (4 and 4). That is 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes per parameter, the accounting of the ZeRO paper (Rajbhandari et al., 2020). It is a baseline, not a law: it explains why state_bytes takes the five sizes as keyword arguments, so that you can ask what an 8-bit optimiser would save.

Activations are the intermediate tensors the forward pass saves for the backward pass. Korthikanti et al. (2022) counted them tensor by tensor for a GPT-style layer in 16-bit numbers: with sequence length s, microbatch b, width h and a heads, one layer saves s · b · h · (34 + 5 · a · s / h) bytes. The 34 s b h part is linear in the sequence; the 5 a s2 b part is the (s, s) attention tables, quadratic in s. Two standard techniques attack the terms. A fused attention kernel (FlashAttention, chapter 19) never stores the (s, s) tables, so the second part vanishes. Recomputation (gradient checkpointing, Chen et al., 2016) stores only each layer's input, 2 s b h bytes, and recomputes the rest in the backward pass at the price of roughly a third more compute. The formula is for a GELU block with full multi-head attention, so for Llama-style blocks treat it as an estimate within tens of per cent, as chapter 16 says.

import solution as m
GB = 1e9
c = m.MODELS["Llama 3 8B"]
print(f"states {m.state_bytes(m.count_params(c)) / GB:.1f} GB")
print(f"{'seq len':>8} {'keep all':>10} {'fused attention':>16} {'recompute':>10}")
for s in (2048, 4096, 8192, 16384):
    print(f"{s:>8} " + " ".join(f"{m.activation_bytes(c, s, 1, mode) / GB:>{w}.1f}" for mode, w in (("full", 7), ("flash", 12), ("recompute", 10))) + " GB")
small = m.Config("1B-class", C=2048, L=20, H=16, KV=16, F=8192, V=32000, mlp="gelu", tied=True)
n = m.count_params(small)
print(f"\n1B-class model: {n / 1e9:.2f} B parameters, states {m.state_bytes(n) / GB:.1f} GB, 24 GB card, 2,048 tokens")
for mode in ("full", "flash", "recompute"):
    print(f"  {mode:<10} largest microbatch: {m.max_microbatch(small, 2048, mode, 24 * GB)}")
print(f"largest model whose states fit 80 GB: {m.max_trainable_params(80 * GB) / GB:.2f} B parameters")
states 128.5 GB
 seq len   keep all  fused attention  recompute
    2048    30.6          9.1        0.5 GB
    4096   104.2         18.3        1.1 GB
    8192   380.1         36.5        2.1 GB
   16384  1447.4         73.0        4.3 GB

1B-class model: 1.07 B parameters, states 17.2 GB, 24 GB card, 2,048 tokens
  full       largest microbatch: 0
  flash      largest microbatch: 1
  recompute  largest microbatch: 22
largest model whose states fit 80 GB: 4.81 B parameters

The first table is chapter 16's. At 4,096 tokens a single sequence wants 104 GB of activations if everything is kept, 18 GB with a fused kernel and 1 GB with full recomputation; at 16,384 tokens, 1.4 terabytes against 73 GB against 4 GB. The 8B model's states (128.5 GB) do not fit an 80 GB card in any of these cases, which is the point: that model needs its states sharded across GPUs (ZeRO and FSDP, A3 chapter 02), and your calculator tells you so before the first rental. The second experiment is the worked example of the chapter: a 1.07-billion-parameter model on a 24 GB card has 17.2 GB of states, so only about 4 GB (after a 3 GB allowance for the CUDA context, buffers and fragmentation) is left for activations. Keeping everything does not fit at all; a fused kernel allows a microbatch of one; recomputation allows 22. The last line is the rule of thumb to remember: an 80 GB card holds the states of a model of at most about 4.8 billion parameters, with nothing left over.

Try it yourself

In demo.py (or an interpreter), ask what an 8-bit optimiser buys you: state_bytes(n, m=1, v=1) is 10 bytes per parameter instead of 16, so the 24 GB card's largest trainable model grows from about 1.3 B to about 2.1 B parameters. Then find the largest microbatch of the 1B-class model at a 4,096-token sequence with each of the three modes. Which technique helped most, and which one would you reach for first on a real run?

$ python3 demo.py solution | head -20

milestones.title: inference, the KV cache and the bandwidth limit
milestones.task: Write kv_bytes_per_token(cfg, bytes_per=2), kv_cache_bytes(cfg, ctx, batch=1, bytes_per=2), weight_bytes(cfg, bytes_per=2), max_batch(cfg, ctx, gpu_mem, ...), decode_step_seconds(cfg, ctx, batch, bw, peak, ...), decode_tokens_per_second and ridge_batch(cfg, bw, peak, w_bytes=2). Every parameter of a mixture of experts must be in weight_bytes, even the idle experts.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks 131,072 and 524,288 bytes per token for Llama 3 8B and Llama 2 7B, the 1.07 GB conversation, 56 and 227 sequences per 80 GB card, 0 for the 70B, 208.6 tokens per second at batch 1 with no context (chapter 16's 209), the 4-times speed-up from 4-bit weights, the compute ceiling for huge batches, the ridge at 316, that throughput never falls as the batch grows, and that below the ridge the step time does not depend on the batch.
milestones.explain:
Serving drops the gradients and the optimiser state: the states shrink to the weights alone, 2 bytes per parameter in bf16 (a quarter of that in 4-bit quantisation, A3 chapter 19). A new item appears. To produce the next token, attention needs the keys and values of every earlier token, and recomputing them for each new token would be wasteful, so they are stored: the KV cache. For each token, in each of the L layers, it holds one key and one value of KV heads times dk numbers:

KV bytes per token = 2 × L × KV × dk × (bytes per number)

For Llama 3 8B in bf16 that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token, about 1.07 GB for one 8,192-token conversation. With full multi-head attention (KV = H = 32, as in Llama 2 7B) the cache is four times larger, 512 KiB per token, which is the reason GQA exists. Memory capacity then limits how many conversations a card can serve at once: the weights are paid once, the cache once for every sequence.

The second constraint is speed. To generate one token the GPU must read every weight (and the sequence's cache) from memory, and it does only 2 FLOPs per weight read. Compare the two ways of spending a step: the memory time, bytes read divided by the memory bandwidth, and the compute time, FLOPs divided by the peak. Whichever is larger sets the step time (the idea of the roofline model of Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009). With one sequence the memory time dominates by a factor of hundreds, so decoding is limited by bytes, not FLOP/s: at 3.35 TB/s an H100 cannot read the 16.1 GB of Llama 3 8B's weights more than about 209 times a second, which is 209 tokens per second for one user, however fast its arithmetic units are. Batching shares the weight reads: with b sequences in the batch, one pass over the weights produces b tokens, so throughput rises almost linearly with b until the arithmetic units become the limit. The batch where the two times are equal is the ridge: batch = peak × weight bytes / (2 × matmul weights × bandwidth), which is 316 for this model on an H100.

import solution as m
GB = 1e9
for name in ("Llama 2 7B", "Llama 3 8B", "Llama 3 70B"):
    c = m.MODELS[name]
    print(f"{name:<12} KV cache {m.kv_bytes_per_token(c) // 1024:>4} KiB/token, {m.kv_cache_bytes(c, 8192) / GB:5.2f} GB for 8,192 tokens, "
          f"bf16 weights {m.weight_bytes(c) / GB:6.1f} GB, 80 GB card holds {m.max_batch(c, 8192, 80 * GB)} such sequences")
c = m.MODELS["Llama 3 8B"]
g = m.GPUS["H100 SXM"]
print(f"\nridge batch (memory-bound below, compute-bound above): {m.ridge_batch(c, g['bw'], g['peak']):.0f}")
print(f"{'batch':>6} {'tokens/s':>10} {'per user':>9}   (context 0, as if the cache were free)")
for b in (1, 8, 64, 316, 1024, 4096):
    t = m.decode_tokens_per_second(c, 0, b, g["bw"], g["peak"])
    print(f"{b:>6} {t:>10,.0f} {t / b:>9.1f}")
Llama 2 7B   KV cache  512 KiB/token,  4.29 GB for 8,192 tokens, bf16 weights   13.5 GB, 80 GB card holds 14 such sequences
Llama 3 8B   KV cache  128 KiB/token,  1.07 GB for 8,192 tokens, bf16 weights   16.1 GB, 80 GB card holds 56 such sequences
Llama 3 70B  KV cache  320 KiB/token,  2.68 GB for 8,192 tokens, bf16 weights  141.1 GB, 80 GB card holds 0 such sequences

ridge batch (memory-bound below, compute-bound above): 316
 batch   tokens/s  per user   (context 0, as if the cache were free)
     1        209     208.6
     8      1,669     208.6
    64     13,350     208.6
   316     65,892     208.5
  1024     65,892      64.3
  4096     65,892      16.1

Read the first block for the capacity story: the 70B model in bf16 needs 141 GB for its weights, so it does not fit one 80 GB card at all, and Llama 2 7B (without GQA) holds 14 conversations beside its weights where Llama 3 8B holds 56. The second block is the bandwidth story: 209 tokens per second for one user, rising in proportion to the batch up to the ridge at 316 sequences and flat at 65,892 tokens a second after it, which is the H100's peak divided by 2 FLOPs per weight. The per-user column shows the trade that every serving system manages: more throughput costs each user speed once the arithmetic is saturated. The next figure plots both lines on log axes.

This is the lesson of the milestone, and the checker prints the same table for a 2,048-token context: batch 1 gives 205 tokens per second, batch 8 gives 1,472, batch 64 gives 6,450 and the largest batch that fits, 227, gives 9,877: about 15% of the compute ceiling. Memory capacity caps the batch before compute does, so the lever for cheaper serving is to shrink bytes: 4-bit weights read a quarter as much, grouped-query attention shrinks the cache by 4 times, and shorter contexts shrink it in proportion.

Systems connection

This is the arithmetic of the roofline model: a kernel is memory-bound when its arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) is below the machine's ratio of peak FLOP/s to bandwidth, here 989 × 1012 / 3.35 × 1012 = 295 FLOPs per byte. A decode step at batch 1 performs 1 FLOP per byte of bf16 weights, hundreds of times too little to keep the arithmetic units busy. The cure is the same as for any memory-bound system: reuse each byte more (batching), or move fewer bytes (quantisation, GQA). Utilisation numbers like MFU play the part of CPU utilisation in queueing theory: a low one tells you to profile, not to buy more machines.

milestones.title: compute-optimal sizes
milestones.task: Write loss(N, D, fit), optimum(C, fit) (returning (N, D, loss)), chinchilla_rule(C, ratio=20) (returning (N, D)), isoflop_loss(C, N, fit) and excess_loss(C, factor, fit). A fit is the tuple (E, A, B, alpha, beta).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the loss formula, the Besiroglu optimum at Gopher's budget (7.225 × 1010 parameters, 1.329 × 1012 tokens), the printed-constants optimum at 1019 FLOPs (2.28 × 108, 32.1 tokens per parameter), the 20-token rule, the chapter's excess-loss table (0.0099 nats at half the optimal size, 0.0408 at four times), and then 30 seeded random fits and budgets: 6ND must equal C exactly, and models 0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1.05, 1.25 and 2 times the optimal size must all have higher loss. That last test checks your closed form without knowing the answer.
milestones.explain:
The first four milestones answer "what does this model cost?". The last two ask the harder question of chapter 18: what should the model be? Given a compute budget C, should you train a bigger model on fewer tokens or a smaller one on more? Hoffmann et al. (2022, "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models") modelled the held-out loss of a language model as

Plug in numbers. The two famous runs, with the constants printed in the paper. Each column is one term above.

The idea

  1. E, A, B, α, β as printed; two runs given as (N, D)
  2. capacity ← A ÷ Nα; data ← B ÷ Dβ
  3. loss ← E + capacity + data; budget ← 6ND
"""L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta with the Hoffmann et al. fit."""

# ── 1. The constants printed in the paper ────────────────────────────────
E, A, B = 1.69, 406.4, 410.7      # floor and the two scales
ALPHA, BETA = 0.34, 0.28          # how fast each penalty shrinks

# ── 2. Two runs with a similar budget: parameters N, tokens D ────────────
RUNS = {"Gopher": (280e9, 300e9), "Chinchilla": (70e9, 1.4e12)}

# ── 3. Each term, then the sum ───────────────────────────────────────────
print(f"{'run':<11}{'C=6ND':>10}{'floor':>7}{'A/N^a':>7}{'B/D^b':>7}"
      f"{'loss':>7}")
for name, (N, D) in RUNS.items():
    capacity = A / N ** ALPHA     # the penalty for having only N weights
    data = B / D ** BETA          # the penalty for seeing only D tokens
    loss = E + capacity + data
    print(f"{name:<11}{6 * N * D:>10.2e}{E:>7.2f}{capacity:>7.3f}"
          f"{data:>7.3f}{loss:>7.3f}")

an irreducible floor E (the entropy of the text), a penalty for having only N parameters, and a penalty for having seen only D tokens. Fix the budget with C = 6ND (so D = C / 6N) and ask which N gives the lowest loss. Setting the derivative with respect to N to zero (the derivation is in a "Go deeper" box of chapter 18) gives a closed form:

Nopt = G · (C/6)β/(α+β),   Dopt = C / (6 Nopt),   G = (αA / βB)1/(α+β)

The constants matter, and chapter 18 told a cautionary story about them: the numbers printed in the Chinchilla paper (E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34, β = 0.28) imply an optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio that rises with budget, contradicting the paper's own "about 20 tokens per parameter"; a replication by Besiroglu et al. (2024) refitted the data and got constants that agree with the paper's other methods. The starter file carries both in FITS so that you can see the difference.

import solution as m
for name, fit in m.FITS.items():
    print(name)
    for C in (1e19, 1e21, 5.76e23, 3.8e25):
        N, D, L = m.optimum(C, fit)
        print(f"  C={C:8.2e}  N={N:9.3e}  D={D:9.3e}  D/N={D / N:5.1f}  loss {L:.3f}")
print("20-tokens-per-parameter rule at 5.76e23:", "N=%.3e D=%.3e" % m.chinchilla_rule(5.76e23))
fit = m.BESIROGLU
print("price of straying from the optimum at C = 1e22 (Besiroglu fit):")
for f in (0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8):
    print(f"  {f:>5} x optimal size: +{m.excess_loss(1e22, f, fit):.4f} nats")

Three observations. First, the printed constants and the refit disagree about the shape of the answer. The printed ones say tokens per parameter should climb from 32 to 139 as the budget grows; the refit says it should stay near 20 and drift down from 24 to 16.5. At Gopher's budget (5.76 × 1023 FLOPs) the refit gives 72 billion parameters on 1.33 trillion tokens, almost exactly what DeepMind trained as Chinchilla (70 billion on 1.4 trillion), while the printed constants give 32 billion on 3 trillion. Quote the finding (about 20 tokens per parameter) and the method, not the third significant digit. Second, the chinchilla_rule shortcut D = 20N with C = 6ND gives N = √(C/120): 69 billion parameters at that budget, the same answer to a few per cent. Third, the bottom of the curve is flat: at a fixed 1022 FLOPs a model half or twice the optimal size costs only about 0.01 nats of loss, and four times about 0.04. That flatness is what gives you freedom to choose a size for other reasons, and milestone 6 uses it.

Common misconception

"Chinchilla says every model should be trained on 20 tokens per parameter." The 20 is the answer to one question: the lowest loss for a fixed training compute, fitted for one data distribution and one family of models. It says nothing about the cost of using the model afterwards. The next milestone makes that cost explicit, and you will see the optimal tokens per parameter move from 18 to over 600 as the expected usage grows.

milestones.explain:
Chinchilla minimises the bill for training. A model that will be queried billions of times has a second bill, and it grows with the size of the model: every token it generates costs about 2N FLOPs (and reads N weights). If two models reach the same loss, the smaller one is cheaper to use forever. Sardana et al. (2023, "Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws") add that cost to the Chinchilla analysis and find that a model with heavy expected usage should be smaller and trained for longer than the compute-optimal one. In this milestone you do their calculation in its simplest form.

Choose a target loss, the quality you need. For any model size N, the fitted law says how many tokens D(N) it takes to reach that loss: solve B / Dβ = target − E − A / Nα for D. If the right-hand side is zero or negative, that N can never reach the target, whatever the data. The lifetime cost of a candidate is then

6 · N · D(N)  +  2 · N · (tokens the model will generate)

and it is a function of N alone. It is enormous just above the smallest feasible size (D explodes) and enormous for large N (6ND explodes), with one minimum between: a one-dimensional search, which you can do by ternary search on log N. With no serving, the minimum is exactly the compute-optimal model for the budget it costs (the checker verifies this against your milestone 5 formula). With serving, the minimum moves to smaller models trained on more data.

The table below is from the demo. All five rows reach the same predicted loss; the first is the Chinchilla-style answer, and the last spends 43 times the training tokens on a model about one fifth the size:

How big should the model be? Target: the loss the Besiroglu fit gives for Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens)
  target loss 1.974
   tokens served    params  train tokens  tokens/param  lifetime FLOPs
           0e+00     73.0B        1.34 T            18        5.88e+23
           1e+12     57.7B        1.73 T            30        7.16e+23
           1e+13     34.5B        3.75 T           109        1.47e+24
           1e+14     21.2B       13.12 T           619        5.90e+24
           1e+15     15.6B       57.74 T          3703        3.66e+25

Read the last column. Lifetime FLOPs are 5.9 × 1023 with no serving and rise as more tokens are served: serving 1013 tokens (about ten billion replies of 1,000 tokens, an assumption you can change) costs 1.47 × 1024 FLOPs in total for the 34-billion-parameter plan, where the compute-optimal 73-billion plan would cost 2.05 × 1024: the checker prints the saving, 28%. At 1015 served tokens the best model is 16 billion parameters seeing 58 trillion tokens, nearly 3,700 tokens per parameter. This is what models intended for heavy use look like: chapter 18's note that Llama 3 405B sits at about 39 tokens per parameter, and that small models in the family train far beyond that ratio, is this calculation done by a company with a large user base. Two honest caveats: the law is fitted on one family of models and one corpus, so it says nothing quantitative about newer data and recipes (chapter 18's state-of-play note), and a real plan must also consider that the data may not exist (Muennighoff et al., 2023, on repeated data). The method, not the constants, is what carries over.
